html:
The Kizil Caves are a set of Buddhist cave temples cut into a cliff above the Muzat river, about 65 km west of Kucha in Xinjiang, western China. They were made and painted between the 3rd and 8th centuries.

Kucha was a rich oasis kingdom on the northern Silk Road route. Its people spoke a Tocharian language and followed Buddhism. Monks carved over two hundred caves here, some for living and meditation, some as shrines.

The murals are the treasure. Painted in bright blues and greens, they show the lives of the Buddha and his past lives, the jataka tales, set in rows of diamond shaped panels. Their style mixes Indian and Iranian art, and they are said to be the earliest major Buddhist cave complex in China. Their model was copied by later caves further east.

A statue of the great translator Kumarajiva, born in Kucha, stands in front of the site. In the early 1900s German expeditions led by Albert von Le Coq cut away many murals and took them to Berlin, where some were destroyed in Second World War bombing.
